lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on poker’s lessons for life
lead.head: Play the hand, not the outcome

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 38

body: Ajay Shah opened with flat­tery. Listeners wanted an episode on poker, he said, “be­cause one of us is a ge­nius and knows a hell of a lot about poker.” {038-J01}

Amit Varma ob­jected. The golden rule, he said, is to un­der­promise and overde­liver. He was no ge­nius, but he had played poker se­ri­ously for many years and loved the game, while hav­ing con­flict­ing thoughts about it.

What fol­lowed was a stripped-down pre­sen­ta­tion on the foun­da­tions of poker, and then a con­ver­sa­tion about what they teach. Poker, Shah said, is a small game hid­ing a metaphor about life, “be­cause life ac­tu­ally is a play of prob­a­bil­ity.”
## The arith­metic of a hand
The first big les­son, Varma said, is ex­pected value. Toss a fair coin: heads, he pays you 51 paise; tails, you pay him 49. Over 100 flips you would be up a paisa a flip, so the bet is “plus EV”.
Lose the toss and you have still cho­sen well. “You made the right de­ci­sion and you got un­lucky,” Varma said. {038-C01}
The same sum de­cides whether to call a bet with a flush draw, and ex­plains why ag­gres­sion pays: a raise that makes a bet­ter hand fold wins the pot too.

Then came game the­ory. A player whose range holds bluffs and value hands in ex­actly the right pro­por­tions can­not lose in the long run, what­ever his op­po­nent holds. It is al­most im­pos­si­ble for a human to play that way, so real poker is a con­test of spot­ting and ex­ploit­ing each other’s de­vi­a­tions.
## A game of the mind
Maths is not the whole of it. “In the­ory, poker is all about the num­bers. In prac­tice, though, it’s a men­tal game,” Varma said. {038-C05}
The enemy is tilt, the anger that turns good play­ers into bad ones. Loss aver­sion feeds it, be­cause a loss hurts more than an equal win pleases.

He ended with a cau­tion. When he started play­ing, he said, only about 5 per cent of play­ers were long-term win­ners. By the time he left, he saw that many win­ners leave, while the losers stay, be­cause they are ad­dicted.
## Three lessons for life
In the con­ver­sa­tion that fol­lowed, Varma drew three lessons from the table. The first is to ac­knowl­edge the role of luck, and then to focus only on what you can con­trol.
The sec­ond is to think prob­a­bilis­ti­cally. Hindsight makes the past look in­evitable, but be­fore a die lands, every num­ber has its chance. {038-C08}
The third is to put in vol­ume. A hand be­tween the world’s best player and a be­gin­ner is roughly 51-49, so the edge shows only over a large sam­ple. {#novice}

Shah had al­ready ar­rived at the same place through fi­nance. Many small bets, each right 51 per cent of the time, beat one big bet held with full con­vic­tion, as long as they are not all drawn from one cor­re­lated idea.

Then Varma named the tragedy. In poker he could play a mil­lion hands. Life often does not allow such a sam­ple, and mostly ev­ery­thing is luck: the skill lies in how well one plays the cards one is dealt.
Where vol­ume is im­pos­si­ble, Shah said, be zen. “Don’t beat your­self up and don’t go rag­ing against life and the world. It just is.”
Varma, think­ing aloud, won­dered how some­body beats them­selves up. Then he signed off: “next time.”

second.label: Poker and finance
second.head: The 51 per cent solution
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for many small bets over one big conviction
body: Ajay Shah car­ried Amit Varma’s poker lessons into fi­nance, cit­ing what he be­lieved was Mark Twain’s line: if you must fore­cast, fore­cast often. {038-J04}

The usual mis­take, Shah said, is to stay cau­tious and com­mit only when ab­so­lutely sure, which he called a delu­sion. Efficient mar­kets the­ory teaches that pric­ing mis­takes are small, so even 51 per cent is hard to reach. Better, then, to hold many small po­si­tions with a 51 per cent chance each than one giant po­si­tion held with full con­vic­tion. {038-C11}

But the law of large num­bers needs in­de­pen­dent draws. Shuffling guar­an­tees that in poker. In fi­nance, one mind­set can make a hun­dred bets flow from one cor­re­lated idea, leav­ing only an il­lu­sion of di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion. {038-C12}

quote.text: So what you can con­trol is the num­ber of ideas. And the ex­tent to which they’re cor­re­lated.

third.head: All bets are on
body: When peo­ple dis­miss poker as gam­bling, Amit Varma has two an­swers. First, it is a game of skill. Second, what is wrong with gam­bling? {038-C09}

If gam­bling means act­ing on prob­a­bilis­tic judge­ments, Varma said, we all do it every day. Crossing the road car­ries a chance of being hit by a truck, greater than the risk of an air ac­ci­dent, and yet we cross. {#truck}
Approach a pretty girl at a bar, and you are weigh­ing a range of pos­si­ble re­sponses. “You buy a house, it’s a gam­ble. You make a friend, it’s a gam­ble,” he said. {#house}

Every ac­tion, with its op­por­tu­nity costs piled up, is a gam­ble. Most of us think prob­a­bilis­ti­cally with­out ad­mit­ting it, he ar­gued, and ad­mit­ting it would help us stop blam­ing our­selves for past de­ci­sions that went wrong.

sections.label: Expected value
sections.head: The coin that pays a paisa
sections.caption: expected value and equity
body: The first big les­son of poker, Amit Varma said, is prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing, and it be­gins with ex­pected value. Offer a fair coin: heads, you win 51 paise; tails, you pay 49. Over 100 flips you ex­pect to be up 100 paise, a paisa a flip, so the bet is plus-EV. {038-C01}
If it lands tails, you were un­lucky, not wrong. Keep mak­ing plus-EV de­ci­sions and you win in the long run.
At the table, say you hold ace-ten of hearts with two hearts on the flop. Nine hearts re­main un­seen, and one of them ar­rives by the river about 38 per cent of the time. {#hearts}

An op­po­nent shoves 10,000 into a 10,000 pot. You must call 10,000 to win 20,000, so you need to be right a third of the time: an easy call. Had he bet 20,000, you would need 40 per cent, and it would be just about a fold.
## Make him fold

Your chance of win­ning ap­plied to the pot is your pot eq­uity. Fold eq­uity is what you win when your raise makes the other player give up, and it can turn a los­ing all-in into a prof­itable one. {038-C02}
So there are two rea­sons to bet: for value, to make a worse hand call, or as a bluff, to make a bet­ter hand fold.
~ Position adds in­for­ma­tion. The player on the dealer but­ton acts last, and the later you act, Varma said, the weaker the hands you can play. {038-C03}

quote.text: You don’t have to make the best hand to win. Making the other guy fold also works.

sections.label: Game theory
sections.head: Bluff by the numbers
sections.caption: game theory and bluffing
body: Watch pop­u­lar cin­ema and you might think poker is all about spot­ting tells and bluffs, Amit Varma said. Apply game the­ory, and you need not even think about your opponent’s cards. {#cinema}

Suppose he bets 100 into a pot of 200 on the river. His op­po­nent gets three to one on a call and must be right 25 per cent of the time to break even. If Varma’s range is ex­actly 25 per cent bluffs and 75 per cent value hands, he can­not lose, what­ever the other player does. {#range}
For a pot-sized bet the right mix is one-third bluffs. A bal­anced range, he said, is not a mix of good and bad hands; it is one with the pro­por­tions right.
In rock, paper, scis­sors, the op­ti­mal strat­egy is to be to­tally ran­dom. In foot­ball, penalty-takers ran­domise, so goal­keep­ers must too. {#rps}
## Exploit, and be ex­ploited

It is al­most im­pos­si­ble for a human to play this game the­ory op­ti­mal, or GTO, poker, so real poker is ex­ploita­tive. If an op­po­nent folded too much, Varma would bluff him more; if he called too much, Varma would bet more for value.

~ Every de­vi­a­tion can be pun­ished, his own in­cluded. {038-C04} A rival who no­ticed him bluff­ing more could start call­ing more. That, he said, is much of the fun: men­tal games of fig­ur­ing each other out.

quote.text: But equally when I am ex­ploita­tive, I am also ex­ploitable be­cause I am also de­vi­at­ing from GTO.

sections.label: The mental game
sections.head: When the maths isn’t enough
sections.caption: tilt and the mental game
body: Human be­ings play poker, Amit Varma said, and human be­ings are frail and flawed. Their weak­ness at the table has a name: tilt, a loss of com­po­sure, usu­ally from anger, that leads to bad de­ci­sions and lost money. {038-C05}

Poker puts an un­usual load on the emo­tions. In most fields a bad day on March 15 is no big deal; in poker it can cost you ev­ery­thing you earned in January and February, es­pe­cially since most play­ers he knows do not man­age their bankroll. {#bankroll}
That can feel dev­as­tat­ing to men whose ego is tied to money as sta­tus and to win­ning. Loss aver­sion makes it worse.
## The en­ti­tled player
Varma’s own weak­ness was en­ti­tle­ment tilt: sit­ting down armed with maths and game the­ory, only to fume at bad beats from play­ers who knew none of it. {038-S02}

His clos­ing cau­tion was about ad­dic­tion. When he started, he said, only about 5 per cent of play­ers were long-term win­ners; by the time he left, he saw that many of them moved on, while the losers stayed. {038-S03}
~ He also urged view­ers to check the law. When he last checked, live poker in India was pos­si­ble only in the off­shore casi­nos of Goa and in Sikkim. {#goa}

quote.text: Mastering the math is not enough. You also have to mas­ter the mind.

sections.label: The first lesson
sections.head: Neither fate nor fault
sections.caption: acknowledging luck
body: Ajay Shah pushed Amit Varma one level be­yond the game. Poker is a small game, he said, but in­side it hides a metaphor about life. Varma replied with three lessons.
The first is to ac­knowl­edge luck. Poker is a game of skill, Varma said, but the quan­tum of luck is so high that the skill lies in man­ag­ing it. Life is no dif­fer­ent. {038-C06}
Misread luck and you pay ei­ther way. Good for­tune makes us ar­ro­gant and com­pla­cent. Bad for­tune makes us de­featist, or gives us im­poster syn­drome.
## Dharma, not des­tiny

The an­swer is not fa­tal­ism. Poker play­ers are taught not to be re­sults-oriented, and Varma reached for a pair­ing: “Lord Krishna and Spike Lee would be in agree­ment over this.” Do the right thing, and don’t worry about the fruits of your ac­tion. {038-J03}
Your dharma, he said, is to do your best and be equani­mous about the rest, al­most in a Buddhist way. Much un­hap­pi­ness comes from not ac­cept­ing con­se­quences we do not con­trol.

~ Nor is bad luck a sign of fate, he said. In his col­umn *Unlikely is Inevitable*, he de­scribed the law of truly large num­bers: with enough it­er­a­tions, the most un­likely things will hap­pen. {038-R04}

quote.text: I would go as far as to say that ninety-eight or ninety-nine per­cent of ev­ery­thing that hap­pens to us is sheer luck.

sections.label: The second lesson
sections.head: The die is still in the air
sections.caption: thinking in probabilities
body: Amit Varma’s sec­ond les­son is to think prob­a­bilis­ti­cally. Hindsight bias makes ev­ery­thing in the past look in­evitable, be­cause once some­thing is over it has ei­ther hap­pened or it hasn’t. {038-C08}
Before that, there were only prob­a­bil­i­ties. A die that lands on five has 100 per cent landed on five, but while it is in the air every num­ber has an even chance.
Nor does the charge that poker is gam­bling trou­ble him. “What’s wrong with gam­bling? We are all gam­bling,” he said. {038-C09} Every ac­tion, with its op­por­tu­nity costs, is a gam­ble.

Admitting this, Varma ar­gued, stops us blam­ing our­selves for past de­ci­sions that went wrong, and putting num­bers on im­por­tant de­ci­sions brings clar­ity about what we are doing and why. {#clarity}
## Shah’s mar­kets

Ajay Shah had pre-empted the point, Varma said, by tak­ing it into mar­kets. Many small bets, each right 51 per cent of the time, work out bet­ter than one big bet held with full con­vic­tion. {038-C11}

~ The catch is in­de­pen­dence. Shuffling guar­an­tees it in poker; in fi­nance, a hun­dred bets can all flow from one cor­re­lated idea. What re­mains, Shah said, “is up to Lady Luck, and then you just should be zen about it.” {038-C12}

quote.text: After some­thing has hap­pened, it has 100% hap­pened or it has zero per­cent hap­pened, which means it’s not hap­pened.

art.caption: Amit Varma on thinking in probabilities

sections.label: The third lesson
sections.head: A million hands, one life
sections.caption: putting in volume
body: The third les­son is to put in vol­ume. Amit Varma would lose a hun­dred points of ten­nis to Nadal, and a hun­dred games of chess to Magnus Carlsen, “even though I’m a good recre­ational player”. {038-J05}
Poker is dif­fer­ent. A hand be­tween the best player in the world and some­one who just learned the rules is about 51-49. {#novice} The edge shows only over a large sam­ple.
So every de­ci­sion should aim to be plus-EV, he said, and a player must stay deeply self-critical, be­cause an as­sump­tion, a premise or the maths may be wrong.
## Doors for cre­ators

For cre­ators, vol­ume pays twice. Constant it­er­a­tion makes you bet­ter, and each new video or blog post is an­other chance of going viral. This does not mean spread­ing your­self ev­ery­where, which Varma called daft, but putting vol­ume into what you are pas­sion­ate about. {038-C13}

Then the tragedy. In poker he could play a mil­lion hands, and at one point he played sev­eral ta­bles at once on­line. Life rarely al­lows such a sam­ple. He and Shah, he said, were dealt in­cred­i­bly good start­ing hands, and their dharma is to make the most of them and help oth­ers. {038-C14}
~ Where high num­bers are not a choice, Shah said, be a lit­tle zen: don’t beat your­self up, and ac­cept those lot­ter­ies.

quote.text: If you have many doors, op­por­tu­nity will knock some­where or the other.

art.caption: Amit Varma on putting in volume

quote.text: The tragic les­son of poker is that mostly ev­ery­thing is luck, and your skill only ap­plies to how well you play the cards that you’re dealt.

p3.title: Tales from the table
p3.deck: Three stories Amit Varma brought back from five serious years of play

stories.kicker: Amit Varma answers a question Ajay Shah once asked him
stories.head: The delusion machine
body: Ajay Shah once asked Amit Varma a ques­tion. Why do bad play­ers bet money on poker, but never on chess? {038-S01}

In chess, Varma an­swered, you get im­me­di­ate feed­back with every game about how good you are. The Elo rat­ings on the major chess sites and in com­pet­i­tive chess are pretty ac­cu­rate, so every player knows his level, and a bad player won’t be stupid enough to bet against a bet­ter one.

Poker is also a game of skill, but luck plays a much big­ger part. In poker terms, the vari­ance is high, and skill shows only in the long run. Every bad player has lucky hands, lucky ses­sions, even lucky months, and many end up be­liev­ing they are good when they are not.
~ Good play­ers guard against this, Varma said. They train them­selves to think in terms of ex­pected value, and keep mak­ing good de­ci­sions with­out wor­ry­ing about short-term out­comes. {#train}
stories.why: Noise hides abil­ity. Where luck is loud and feed­back is slow, peo­ple mis­take good for­tune for skill. Applied to life, Varma said, think­ing in prob­a­bil­i­ties helps us de­cide bet­ter and makes us equani­mous about out­comes. {038-C07}
stories.postscript: So strong is that de­tach­ment, he sug­gested, that un­der­stand­ing poker could be “the route to Buddhism”.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the kind of tilt that undid his maths
stories.head: Undone by a Diwali amateur
body: Amit Varma knows tilt from the in­side. Of its many kinds, the one he was per­son­ally prone to is called en­ti­tle­ment tilt. {038-S02}
He would go into a game armed with all his maths, his game the­ory and his knowl­edge of ranges. Across the table might sit a player who knew none of it, treat­ing poker as a fes­tive card game.
In Varma’s words: “some idiot who knows none of this and is play­ing it like Teen Patti on Diwali would give me five bad beats in a hand and I played cor­rectly.” {038-J02}
Then, he said, he would be fum­ing, and would ac­tu­ally start play­ing badly and los­ing money.
~ There are many kinds of tilt, he added, and a player needs to know what they all are and watch out for them in him­self. All the cog­ni­tive bi­ases come into play too.
stories.why: Knowing the cor­rect play does not pro­tect you from how you react to a bad out­come. Believing you de­serve to win be­cause you did things right is a trap of its own: the mind needs mas­ter­ing too. {038-C05}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what five years at the tables taught him
stories.head: The winners cash out
body: Amit Varma played poker se­ri­ously be­tween 2010 and 2015, and even wrote a reg­u­lar col­umn on it for the *Economic Times*. {#years}

When he started, he fell in love with the math­e­mat­i­cal side of the game. Looking at the ecosys­tem, he saw that only about 5 per cent of play­ers were long-term win­ners. He as­sumed that over a long pe­riod those win­ners would stay in the game and the losers would ro­tate out. {038-S03}

By the time he left, years later, he had re­alised the op­po­site was true. Many win­ners move on, be­cause the qual­i­ties that make them good at poker serve them else­where. The losers stay, be­cause they are ad­dicted.
Gambling ad­dic­tion, he said, is “a ter­ri­ble, ter­ri­ble thing”, and he has seen lives de­stroyed by it.
~ His ad­vice was plain: if you think you have an ad­dic­tive per­son­al­ity, be care­ful, and don’t play this game.

quote.text: Many win­ning play­ers leave be­cause what makes them good at poker also makes them good at other things, so they move on.

stories.postscript: His final col­umn for the *Economic Times*, *Why I Loved and Left Poker*, may, he said, tell you why you shouldn’t start play­ing. {038-R02}

quiz.q: Heads you win 51 paise, tails you pay 49. What is the bet’s expected value per flip?
quiz.a: One paisa a flip: a plus-EV bet, worth tak­ing even if you lose.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, do bad players bet on poker but never on chess?
quiz.a: Chess rat­ings tell ev­ery­one their level; poker’s high vari­ance lets bad play­ers think they’re good.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of equity Varma described in his presentation?
quiz.a: Pot eq­uity, your chance of win­ning ap­plied to the pot, and fold eq­uity.

quiz.q: What kind of tilt was Amit Varma personally prone to at the poker table?
quiz.a: Entitlement tilt: fum­ing at bad beats from play­ers who knew none of the maths.

quiz.q: Which three lessons for life did Varma draw from his years of playing poker?
quiz.a: Acknowledge the role of luck, think prob­a­bilis­ti­cally, and put in vol­ume.

quiz.q: What hidden condition must hold, Ajay Shah warned, for many small bets to work?
quiz.a: The bets must be in­de­pen­dent; cor­re­lated ideas only cre­ate an il­lu­sion of di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 38. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Rafael Nadal (Barcex, CC BY-SA 4.0); Mark Twain (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Unlikely is Inevitable
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn on the law of truly large num­bers: with a big enough sam­ple, un­likely runs are bound to hap­pen, so los­ing sev­eral hands in a row as an 80% favourite is nei­ther a rigged game nor proof of a bad de­ci­sion, and bad luck shouldn’t be read as fate.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Mohit Satyanand on cognitive biases in poker and investing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Mohit Satyanand
shelf.why: Mohit Satyanand on the cog­ni­tive bi­ases poker and in­vest­ing share, and on poker-style prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing ap­plied to mar­kets.

shelf.title: Amit Varma’s Poker Column for the Economic Times (archive)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The ar­chive of the poker col­umn Amit wrote for the Economic Times, in which he ap­plied poker’s prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing be­yond the table: the full body of his poker writ­ing for read­ers who want to go deeper.

shelf.title: Om Namah Volume
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: One of Amit’s poker col­umns, on his life les­son to ‘put in volume’: a small edge pays off only over a large sam­ple.

shelf.title: Luck is All Around
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A short, vivid case for how much luck lies be­hind your ex­is­tence and ev­ery­thing else, and the life les­son that fol­lows: don’t let good luck make you ar­ro­gant or bad luck make you de­featist.

shelf.title: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma
shelf.why: Ajay’s deep dive into the bot­tom-up story of Unix and free soft­ware, built by peo­ple work­ing for decades with no promised re­ward.

laughs.text: On en­ti­tle­ment tilt, Amit de­scribes the op­po­nent who ruins his math-perfect game: ‘some idiot who knows none of this and is play­ing it like Teen Patti on Diwali’. Teen Patti is the ca­sual card game played at Diwali.

On skill vs luck: Amit would lose all of a hun­dred ten­nis points to Nadal and a hun­dred chess games to Magnus Carlsen, ‘even though I’m a good recre­ational player’. But a hand of poker be­tween the world’s best player and ‘some­one who just learned the rules, maybe some­one who just watched my presentation’ is about 51-49.
The dead­pan end­ing. Picking up on Ajay’s ad­vice not to beat your­self up, Amit muses aloud: ‘How does some­body beat them­selves up?’ After a pause from Ajay, he signs off: ‘next time.’

Amit on not being re­sults-oriented: ‘Lord Krishna and Spike Lee would be in agree­ment over this. Do the right thing, don’t worry about the fruits of your ac­tion.’ The line pairs the Gita’s teach­ing on ac­tion with Spike Lee’s film title.
Ajay cites Mark Twain (‘I think’) as say­ing ‘if you must fore­cast, fore­cast often’, and uses it to argue for many small bets over rare high-conviction ones.
Amit says films and pop­u­lar cul­ture ‘com­pletely get it wrong’. They make poker look like a game of spot­ting tells and bluffs, when the foun­da­tion is math and game the­ory.

Game the­ory be­yond poker: in rock-paper-scissors the op­ti­mal strat­egy is to be to­tally ran­dom. In foot­ball penal­ties, good goal­keep­ers know the taker’s stats, so good tak­ers ran­domise, which forces goal­keep­ers to ran­domise too.

Last year’s World Series of Poker Main Event, the de facto world cham­pi­onship: a $10,000 entry fee, 60,000 start­ing tour­na­ment chips, blinds climb­ing from 100/200 to mil­lions, a prize pool of around $95 mil­lion and a first prize of about $12 mil­lion. Amit uses it to il­lus­trate how tour­na­ments work.
